periods.activity_title: Folding to Find: What Is a Line of Symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.219
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.1 p.219
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each of five given polygon figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if any exist.

time_bands.activity: Open with Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1 p.219) ("Do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures….") — students examine the flower, butterfly, rangoli, and pinwheel images and share observations about parts that repeat or mirror each other. Elicit the word 'symmetry' from students; hold the cloud image for contrast.

Demonstrate folding a triangle along a dotted line; students observe that the two halves overlap exactly — these are 'mirror halves'. Then fold the four-puzzle-piece figure; students observe the halves do not overlap. Guide students to articulate the definition: a line of symmetry cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1 p.219) ("For each of five given polygon figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry…."). They fold or trace each polygon figure and mark any line of symmetry they find, recording their results.

Pairs share their answers for Q2; class discusses disagreements. Return to the cloud from Q1 — does it have a line of symmetry? Consolidate: a line of symmetry must produce exact overlap on folding; irregular shapes and the cloud do not have one.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly draw a line that visually 'looks central' but does not produce exact overlap — insist on the physical or imagined fold test as the only criterion. Figure it Out Q2 includes both symmetric and asymmetric polygons, giving immediate contrast. Watch for students who claim the cloud is symmetric; use it to reinforce that symmetry requires exact, not approximate, overlap.
materials: Plain paper squares and rectangles for folding
Printed or textbook copies open to section 9.1 p.219

textbook_segments.ref: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_segments.title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Four Folds: Discovering Multiple Lines of Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Folding a square — finding all lines of symmetry, section 9.1 p.220
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students take a square piece of paper and fold it four times (vertically, horizontally, along each diagonal) to discover that a square has four lines of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

time_bands.activity: Each student receives a square sheet of paper. Ask: 'How many ways can you fold this square so the two halves overlap perfectly?' Students predict silently, then write their guess on the corner of the sheet.

Activity: Folding a square — finding all lines of symmetry (section 9.1 p.220) ("Students take a square piece of paper and fold it four times…."). Students fold vertically, horizontally, and along each diagonal in turn, pressing each fold firmly and checking for exact overlap. They mark each fold line on a traced outline of the square and label the four lines.

Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap?…"). Class discusses whether any additional fold lines exist and confirms the count is four. Students note that multiple lines of symmetry are possible.

Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry?…"). Students fold a non-square rectangle along its diagonal and observe that the triangular halves do not overlap the full rectangle — so the diagonal is NOT a line of symmetry. Contrast with the square to consolidate: having a diagonal does not guarantee a line of symmetry.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is assuming that any line passing through the centre of a figure is a line of symmetry; the rectangle's diagonal fold directly exposes this misconception — make it the anchor of the closing discussion. Having established that a line of symmetry requires exact overlap when folded, students now discover that a single figure can carry several such lines. For self-study, the worked detail in the section's prose on labelling corners A, B, C, D under reflection is a useful follow-up students can read independently.
materials: Square sheets of paper (one per student)

textbook_segments.ref: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_segments.title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Reflection Logic: Why Does the Diagonal Fail?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

time_bands.activity: Draw a labelled square (corners A, B, C, D) on the board. Ask students to trace where corner B lands when the square is folded along the vertical line of symmetry. Establish that B maps to A and C maps to D — this mapping is called reflection. Repeat the reasoning for the horizontal fold.

Using Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap?…"), guide students to reason about the diagonal fold of the square: which corner maps to which? Does the shape after folding look the same? Students write a one- or two-sentence justification for why each fold of the square is a genuine line of symmetry, using the corner-mapping argument.

Return to Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry?…"). Students draw a non-square rectangle, label its corners, and reason: when folded along the diagonal, where does each corner go? They write a brief argument explaining why the corner positions do not coincide with the rectangle's outline — so the diagonal cannot be a line of symmetry.

Class shares justifications. Consolidate: a line of symmetry must reflect every point of the figure onto another point of the same figure — it is not enough to look central. Students with different figures from the previous unit confirm whether the same reasoning applies to their polygons.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often accept a fold line as symmetric if 'most' of the shape overlaps; the corner-labelling argument makes precision mandatory and exposes the rectangle-diagonal error at the level of reasoning, not just visual inspection. Watch for students who reason only about area overlap rather than point-by-point correspondence — direct them back to the corner labels. For a challenge, ask students to find a non-square, non-rectangular quadrilateral that has at least one line of symmetry and justify their answer.
materials: Squared or plain paper for drawing labelled figures

textbook_segments.title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Ink, Fold, Cut: Making Symmetric Shapes by Hand

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Ink Blot Devils, section 9.1 p.222
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together, and open to observe the symmetric figure formed, identifying the fold as the line of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Paper Folding and Cutting, section 9.1 p.223
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students fold paper and cut along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes; a more intricate variant uses multiple folds to create decorative cut-out patterns with identifiable lines of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.224
textbook_items_in_class.description: In each of four figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet and then unfolded. Identify the fold line. For figure (d), created by a single punch, determine how the paper was folded.

time_bands.activity: Activity: Ink Blot Devils (section 9.1 p.222) ("Students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together…."). Each student folds a sheet, drops a small amount of ink or paint on one half, presses the halves together firmly, then opens to reveal the blot figure. Students draw an arrow pointing to the fold line and label it 'line of symmetry'.

Activity: Paper Folding and Cutting (section 9.1 p.223) ("Students fold paper and cut along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes…."). Students follow the dotted-line cuts shown in the textbook, first with a single fold, then with a double fold. They open each cut piece, identify all lines of symmetry, and predict — before opening — what shape the cut will produce.

Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1 p.224) ("In each of four figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet…."). Students examine the four unfolded hole-patterns and work backwards: which fold line would have produced this pattern? They mark the fold lines on each figure and for figure (d) write a sentence explaining the folding method.

Quick whole-class check: a volunteer explains how figure (d) must have been folded. Establish the key insight: the fold line is always a line of symmetry of the resulting pattern, so working backwards from a symmetric pattern reveals the fold.

periods.teacher_notes: The ink-blot step is deliberately short — its role is to make the production of symmetry visceral and memorable before the more precise cutting work. Watch for students who cut without folding first and end up with asymmetric shapes; redirect them to fold before cutting. Figure it Out Q1's reverse task (identifying the fold from the hole pattern) is a strong check of understanding — a student who cannot do it has not yet internalised the fold-symmetry connection.
materials: Ink or washable paint and droppers or small brushes

textbook_segments.ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_segments.title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Predict, Punch, Prove: Symmetric Hole Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Punching Game, section 9.1 p.223
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students punch holes at different locations of a folded square sheet to create symmetric patterns, using the fold as the line of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.1 p.224
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the location of the other hole(s) in each of five figures.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.1 p.225
textbook_items_in_class.description: After each of four cuts on folded paper, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened; make cutouts to verify predictions — sub-parts (a), (b), (c), (d).

time_bands.activity: Activity: Punching Game (section 9.1 p.223) ("Students punch holes at different locations of a folded square sheet…."). Each student folds a square sheet along one axis, punches a hole at a chosen location, predicts where the second hole will appear on the unfolded sheet, then opens and checks. Repeat with a two-fold version: fold twice, punch one hole, predict the number and positions of holes before opening.

Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1 p.224) ("Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the location of the other hole(s)…."). Students work through each of the five figures: given one hole and one or two lines of symmetry, they mark where all reflected holes must appear. They reason about distances from the fold line and use their own square sheets to verify.

Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.1 p.225) ("After each of four cuts on folded paper, predict the shape of the hole…."). For each sub-part, students first predict in writing what shape the opened hole will be, then make the actual cut-out to verify. Predictions and outcomes are compared — discrepancies become a discussion point.

Whole-class consolidation: ask students which sub-part of Q4 surprised them most and why. Emphasise the principle — the shape of the hole when unfolded is always symmetric about the fold line, so understanding the fold fully determines the outcome.

periods.teacher_notes: The most productive error to watch for is students placing the reflected hole on the wrong side of the fold line — have them measure the perpendicular distance from the hole to the fold and reproduce that distance on the other side. Figure it Out Q4's prediction-then-verify structure is intentional: students who skip the prediction step miss the reasoning practice, so encourage written predictions before any cutting. For self-study, Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.1 p.224) on vertical and horizontal fold notation is a readable extension students can tackle independently.
materials: Hole punch or sharp pencil for punching
Rulers for measuring distances from fold

periods.activity_title: Completing and Counting: Symmetric Figures on Grids

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.1 p.226
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how to obtain each of two shapes (both with a square hole in the centre) using folds and a single straight cut — sub-parts (a) aligned-square hole and (b) diamond-orientation square hole.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.1 p.226
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) two figures — a 4-pointed star (square) and an 8-pointed star; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six partial figures on squared paper and complete each so that the given blue line is a line of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f), with a hint to rotate the book for (c) and (f).

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.1 p.226) ("Determine how to obtain each of two shapes…using folds and a single straight cut…."). Students examine the two target shapes — aligned-square hole and diamond-orientation square hole — and work out the sequence of folds and the single cut that would produce each. They sketch the folding steps beside each figure.

Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.1 p.226) ("How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have?…."). Students count lines of symmetry for the 4-pointed star, 8-pointed star, equilateral triangle, and regular hexagon. They draw each line on a traced copy and record the count, noticing that the number of lines relates to the regularity and number of points or sides.

Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.1 p.228) ("Copy six partial figures on squared paper and complete each so that the given blue line is a line of symmetry…."). Students copy each partial figure onto squared paper, identify the given line of symmetry, then reflect each plotted point across that line to complete the figure. For sub-parts (c) and (f) they rotate their book as the textbook hints, then reflect.

Students swap papers with a neighbour and fold along the drawn line of symmetry to check whether the completed figures overlap exactly. Any mismatch is corrected. Consolidate: the grid makes the reflection precise — each point moves the same number of squares perpendicular to the line.

periods.teacher_notes: A recurring error in Q11 is reflecting along the wrong axis — students sometimes reflect diagonally when the line is vertical, or vice versa. Insist on counting grid squares perpendicular to the line of symmetry, not diagonally. Figure it Out Q6 invites students to notice that regular polygons with n sides have n lines of symmetry — if this pattern emerges in discussion, affirm it as a conjecture to revisit later in the chapter. For extended practice, Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1 p.229) is a natural follow-on students can attempt independently.

textbook_segments.title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Drawing with Constraints: Triangles, Hexagons, and Kolam

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.1 p.227
textbook_items_in_class.description: Trace each of eight figures (arrangements of rhombus shapes and polygons on grids) and draw the lines of symmetry, if any.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the lines of symmetry for the given kolam (traditional Indian dot pattern).

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw: (a) a triangle with exactly one line of symmetry; (b) a triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry; (c) a triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw figures containing at least one curved boundary with exactly: (a) one line of symmetry; (b) two lines of symmetry; (c) four lines of symmetry.

homework.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 9.1 p.229
homework.description: Copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f).

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.1 p.227) ("Trace each of eight figures…and draw the lines of symmetry, if any."). Students trace the rhombus and polygon arrangements onto their paper and draw any lines of symmetry they can find. For figures with no line of symmetry, they write a brief note explaining why.

Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.1 p.228) ("Find the lines of symmetry for the given kolam…."). Students examine the kolam pattern and mark all lines of symmetry directly on the textbook figure or a traced copy. Class discussion: how many did you find, and how did you check each one?

Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1 p.228) ("Draw: (a) a triangle with exactly one line of symmetry…."). Students draw each required triangle type and write a one-sentence justification for each. For the question about whether exactly two lines of symmetry is possible, students reason and record their conclusion with an argument.

Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.1 p.228) ("Draw figures containing at least one curved boundary…."). Students produce original drawings with curved boundaries — a half-circle, a leaf shape, a petal — ensuring the exact number of lines of symmetry required. Volunteers share under the visualiser or on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning challenge in Q9 is the question about whether exactly two lines of symmetry is possible for a triangle — students who try to construct one will find it impossible, and the class argument about why (having two lines forces a third) is the conceptual prize of this unit. For Q10, students often draw figures that look symmetric but have one more or fewer lines than required; prompt them to check each claimed line by the fold test. Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1 p.229) is set as homework to extend the two-line symmetry completion work.

textbook_segments.title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry

periods.activity_title: Dot Grids and Segment Extensions: Building Symmetric Figures

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 9.1 p.229
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f).

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 9.1 p.230
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six figures on a dot grid and for each draw two more line segments to make a shape that has a line of symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1 p.229) ("Copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry…."). Students copy each partial figure and complete it so that BOTH given lines are simultaneously lines of symmetry. They work sub-part by sub-part, checking after each: fold along each line in turn and verify overlap.

Figure it Out Q13 (section 9.1 p.230) ("Copy six figures on a dot grid and for each draw two more line segments…."). Students copy each dot-grid figure and add exactly two line segments to create a shape that has at least one line of symmetry. Multiple valid answers exist; students compare solutions with a partner and check each other's lines.

Gallery moment: selected solutions from Q12 and Q13 are shared on the board. For one Q12 sub-part, the class verifies both lines of symmetry together. For Q13, two contrasting solutions for the same figure are shown — both valid — reinforcing that symmetric shapes are not unique.

periods.teacher_notes: The challenge in Q12 is that satisfying two simultaneous lines of symmetry is more constrained than satisfying one — students who complete only one line correctly and ignore the second produce asymmetric figures. Encourage them to apply each fold test separately and then together. Q13's open-ended nature rewards creative thinking; watch for students who add segments that create only near-symmetric figures and guide them back to the fold test. For self-study, Figure it Out Q11 sub-parts (c) and (f) (section 9.1 p.228), which require rotating the book for a diagonal axis, are a useful independent challenge if students have not yet attempted them.
materials: Dot-grid paper or printed dot grids (for Q13)

periods.activity_title: The Spinning Windmill: Introducing Rotational Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point — sub-parts (a), (b), (c).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?

time_bands.activity: Show a paper windmill (or a drawn image). Ask: 'Does this windmill have a line of symmetry?' Students investigate by folding or by reasoning — they discover it does not. Now spin or rotate the image 90°: 'Does it look the same?' Introduce the definitions: the centre of rotation is the fixed point about which the figure is rotated; an angle of symmetry is any angle of rotation for which the figure looks identical. Students record both definitions in their own words.

Examine the square with labelled corners A, B, C, D. Students rotate the square 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°, tracking which corner goes where each time. They list all four angles of symmetry and confirm that 360° is always included. Then examine the windmill: students determine its four angles of symmetry (90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) by the same method.

Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2 p.235) ("Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point…."). Students work through sub-parts (a), (b), and (c), listing every angle at which each figure coincides with its original position. They check: is 360° always present? What is the smallest angle for each?

Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2 p.235) ("Which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?"). Students scan the seven figures and identify those with multiple angles of symmetry, recording which angles apply. Class shares findings to close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse line of symmetry with rotational symmetry — the windmill's lack of reflection symmetry despite clear rotational symmetry is the conceptual pivot; spend time on this contrast. A common error is omitting 360° from the list of angles of symmetry; establish early that every figure that has any rotational symmetry has 360° as an angle, because a full turn always returns a figure to itself. For self-study, the parallelogram-strip worked example (Example, section 9.2 p.232) is a readable illustration of a figure that has NO rotational symmetry.
materials: Paper windmill model or printed windmill image
Labelled square cutout for rotation demonstration

periods.activity_title: Radial Arms and the 360°/n Rule: Building the Generalisation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Paper cutout rotation — three-arm radial figure, section 9.2 p.233
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students trace and cut out a three-arm radial figure, then rotate the cutout over the original figure to determine its angles of rotation and verify observations about rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 9.2 p.232
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angles of symmetry of a parallelogram-strip shape. A 180° rotation is demonstrated not to overlap with the original (asymmetry of the parallelogram); the figure returns to itself only after 360°, so it does not have rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.236
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each of six figures (including an arrow, X-shape, star, tumbling figure, plus-shape, and pentagon).

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example (section 9.2 p.232) ("Find the angles of symmetry of a parallelogram-strip shape….") together as a class. Students see that a 180° rotation does not coincide — the parallelogram's slant means the arms point in the wrong direction — so only 360° qualifies. Students state in their own words: having arms is not sufficient; the arms must be equally spaced for smaller angles to work.

Activity: Paper cutout rotation — three-arm radial figure (section 9.2 p.233) ("Students trace and cut out a three-arm radial figure…."). Students trace the figure, cut it out, and physically rotate the cutout over the printed original, recording every angle at which the cutout coincides exactly. They discover that evenly-spaced three arms give 120°, 240°, 360°. They then reason: 360° ÷ 3 = 120° — the spacing determines the angle.

Class builds the generalisation: for n equally-spaced radial arms, the smallest angle of symmetry is 360°/n and all angles of symmetry are multiples of this value. Students apply this to 4-arm (90°), 5-arm (72°), and 6-arm (60°) figures by calculation, and check whether 7 arms give a whole-number angle (they do not — 51 3/7°). Students record the True/False principle: the smallest whole-number angle of symmetry must be a factor of 360.

Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2 p.236) ("Give the order of rotational symmetry for each of six figures…."). Students begin the six figures; any unfinished parts are noted for independent completion. 'Order of rotational symmetry' is introduced as the count of angles of symmetry that are less than 360°.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical reasoning step is distinguishing equally-spaced arms (which give rotational symmetry) from unequally-spaced arms (which do not); the irregular three-arm figure in the textbook's prose is a useful contrast to show alongside the regular one. Students often assume any figure with rotation symmetry must also have reflection symmetry — the windmill from the preceding unit is the counterexample to keep available. For a challenge, ask students why 7 equally-spaced arms cannot produce a whole-number angle of symmetry and what that implies about the factor relationship.
materials: Printed or traced three-arm radial figure for cutting
Ruler and protractor for checking angles

periods.activity_title: The Perfect Symmetric Shape: Exploring the Circle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has (i) 3 angles of symmetry, (ii) 4 angles of symmetry; (iii) determine all possible numbers of angles of symmetry obtainable by colouring sectors.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw two figures (other than a circle and a square) that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry?

time_bands.activity: Ask students to fold a circular paper disc. Which folds produce exact overlap? Students discover that any fold through the centre works — every diameter is a line of symmetry. Then rotate the disc: at what angles does it coincide with itself? Every angle works. Establish: a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry (every diameter) and every angle of rotation is an angle of symmetry when rotating about the centre.

Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2 p.238) ("Colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has (i) 3 angles of symmetry…."). Students colour the 12-sector diagram to achieve each required count. For (iii), they reason systematically about which divisors of 12 are achievable — recording each valid colouring pattern and the number of angles it produces.

Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2 p.238) ("Draw two figures…that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry."). Students draw their two figures, label the lines of symmetry and state the angles of symmetry for each. They confirm that each figure passes both tests — fold test and rotation test.

Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2 p.238) ("In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry?"). Students apply the generalisation from the radial-arm reasoning: all angles of symmetry are multiples of 60°, up to and including 360°. They list all six: 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°. A brief discussion connects this to a 6-arm or 6-sided regular figure.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes state that a circle has 'no' rotational symmetry because they cannot count a finite number of angles — clarify that every angle of rotation qualifies, which is a special case of the chapter's definition, not an exception to it. Q1's part (iii) is the deepest reasoning in this unit: students must think about which divisors of 12 can actually be realised by a colouring pattern, not just listed as divisors. For real-world connection, ask students to name objects around them (ceiling fans, flowers, wheels) and identify their angles of symmetry.
materials: Pencils and colours for sector diagrams

periods.activity_title: Angle Reasoning: Smallest Angles, Factors, and Feasibility

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: (a) 45°? (b) 17°?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw rough sketches of: (a) a triangle with ≥2 lines and ≥2 angles of symmetry; (b) a triangle with exactly 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry; (c) a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry; (d) a quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but no rotational symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.2 p.238) ("In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°…."). Students reason deductively: if 60° is an angle of symmetry and there are two angles smaller than 60°, those angles must be divisors of 60° that are also factors of 360°. Students list candidates — 30°, 20° — and check which give the required count of angles below 60°. They arrive at the smallest angle and justify their answer in writing.

Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2 p.238) ("Can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: (a) 45°? (b) 17°?"). Students apply the principle that the smallest whole-number angle must be a factor of 360. They check 45: 360 ÷ 45 = 8 — a whole number, so yes. They check 17: 360 ÷ 17 is not a whole number, so no. Students write a one-sentence rule: the smallest angle of symmetry must be a factor of 360°.

Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2 p.238) ("Draw rough sketches of: (a) a triangle with ≥2 lines and ≥2 angles of symmetry…."). Students sketch each of the four required figures, labelling lines of symmetry and stating angles of symmetry. For (c) the quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry, students reason about what shape could work (e.g., a parallelogram, if it has 180° rotation but no line of symmetry) and justify their sketch.

Quick share: one student explains their answer to (c) — the quadrilateral with rotational but no reflection symmetry — and the class checks it using both the fold test and the rotation argument. Consolidate: reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent properties; a figure can have one without the other.

periods.teacher_notes: Q5 is the most demanding deductive reasoning item in this section: students must work backwards from 'two angles less than 60°' to identify the smallest angle, rather than forward from a given smallest angle. Watch for the shortcut error of guessing 20° without checking that it is indeed a factor of 360. The contrast in Q3 between (c) and (d) — rotational without reflection vs. reflection without rotational — is the deepest conceptual distinction of the chapter; both sketches should be validated carefully in class.

periods.activity_title: Regular Polygons, Ashoka Chakra, and Koch Snowflake: Symmetry Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: Parliament Building in Delhi: (a) Does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry — how many lines? (b) Does it have rotational symmetry about its centre — find the angles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many angles of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry do the shapes in the Koch Snowflake sequence (Chapter 1, Table 3) have?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does the Ashoka Chakra have?

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2 p.239) ("Parliament Building in Delhi: (a) Does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry…."). Students examine the Parliament Building image in the textbook, identify lines of symmetry (3, for the circular parliament) and determine the angles of rotational symmetry (120°, 240°, 360°). They write brief answers for both parts.

Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.2 p.239) ("How many lines of symmetry do the Regular Polygons….") and Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.2 p.239) ("How many angles of symmetry do the Regular Polygons…."). Students complete both tables: for an n-sided regular polygon, both the number of lines of symmetry and the number of angles of symmetry equal n. They identify the number sequences (1, 2, 3, 4, …) and record the pattern.

Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.2 p.239) ("How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry do the shapes in the Koch Snowflake sequence…."). Students work through the Koch Snowflake stages from the textbook's table, counting lines and angles of symmetry at each stage. They notice whether the count stays the same or changes as the snowflake becomes more intricate.

Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.2 p.239) ("How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does the Ashoka Chakra have?"). Students count the Ashoka Chakra's 24 spokes, deduce 24 lines of symmetry and 24 angles of symmetry (smallest: 360°/24 = 15°), and list a selection of the angles. Class discusses the connection: the Ashoka Chakra resembles a regular 24-gon in its symmetry properties.

periods.teacher_notes: The regular-polygon questions (Q8 and Q9) are the empirical confirmation of the 360°/n formula developed in the radial-arm reasoning — students should see that the pattern they derived from radial arms holds exactly for regular polygons. For the Koch Snowflake, the key observation is that each iteration preserves the three-fold symmetry of the equilateral triangle, so the count does not change even as the boundary becomes more complex. The Ashoka Chakra question connects mathematics to Indian cultural heritage and is worth a moment's appreciation before moving on.
materials: Chapter 1 Table 3 (regular polygons and Koch Snowflake) accessible for reference

periods.activity_title: Playing with Tiles: Designing Symmetric Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Playing with Tiles, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students use colour tiles to complete a figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry, then use 16 tiles to create figures with exactly 1 or 2 lines of symmetry, and make creative symmetric designs.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw two figures (other than a circle and a square) that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Distribute sets of 16 colour tiles (or coloured squares cut from paper) to each student or pair. Pose the challenge: 'Arrange tiles in a grid so that the arrangement has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.' Students begin experimenting.

Activity: Playing with Tiles (section 9.2 p.239) ("Students use colour tiles to complete a figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry…."). Students first complete the given partial tile figure to achieve exactly 2 lines of symmetry. Then, using all 16 tiles freely, they create one arrangement with exactly 1 line of symmetry and another with exactly 2 lines. For each, they mark the line(s) of symmetry with a pencil line on their squared-paper record.

Students choose their most creative 16-tile design and check whether it also has rotational symmetry — what angles? They record any angles of symmetry on the squared-paper record alongside the lines. Students who finish early attempt to create a design with rotational symmetry but no line of symmetry.

Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2 p.238) ("Draw two figures…that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry."). If not completed in unit 11, students draw and label their two figures here, confirming both symmetry types. Selected tile designs are shown on the board; the class identifies lines and angles of symmetry for each displayed design. Consolidate: a single geometric figure can carry both reflection and rotational symmetry, either, or neither.

periods.teacher_notes: The tile activity is open-ended by design — resist the urge to show a 'correct' completed arrangement early, as the exploration phase produces the learning. Watch for students who create arrangements with more lines of symmetry than required and guide them to reduce the count deliberately. The closing board display, where the class identifies symmetries in each other's designs, serves as a natural consolidation of the chapter's two central concepts without requiring a separate review exercise.
materials: Colour tiles or coloured paper squares (16 per student or pair)

items.prompt: Which of the following best describes a line of symmetry of a two-dimensional figure?

options.label: A
options.text: A line that passes through the centre of the figure

options.label: B
options.text: A line that divides the figure into two parts of equal area

options.label: C
options.text: A line along which the figure can be folded so that both halves overlap exactly

options.label: D
options.text: A line that is parallel to one side of the figure

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — A line along which the figure can be folded so that both halves overlap exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition of line of symmetry: folding along the line must produce exact overlap of both halves.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses 'passing through the centre' with the fold-overlap criterion; a diagonal of a non-square rectangle passes through the centre but is not a line of symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks equal area is sufficient; a rectangle's diagonal splits it into equal areas but the triangular halves do not overlap the rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates a line of symmetry with a line parallel to a side, which is a spatial relationship but carries no symmetry guarantee.

inclusivity.support: Let the student fold a paper triangle to physically check which line produces exact overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name one figure for which a line through the centre is NOT a line of symmetry, and explain why.

exercise.description: Do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?

items.section_title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry
items.prompt: A square has exactly how many lines of symmetry?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 4. The square has lines of symmetry along its vertical axis, horizontal axis, and both diagonals.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the square four ways — vertically, horizontally, and along each diagonal — and confirm that each fold produces exact overlap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student found only the vertical and horizontal lines and did not test the two diagonal folds.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student found only one fold line, likely the vertical, and stopped exploring.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-counted, possibly confusing the square's lines of symmetry with those of a regular octagon or an 8-pointed star.

inclusivity.support: Provide a paper square and guide the student to fold it each of the four ways in turn, checking overlap after each fold.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to sketch another quadrilateral that has exactly 2 lines of symmetry and justify their sketch.

exercise.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

items.prompt: A paper windmill has rotational symmetry with a smallest angle of symmetry of 90°. Which list gives ALL its angles of symmetry?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. All multiples of 90° up to and including 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle (90°) up to and including 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student omits 360°, not yet accepting that a full rotation always returns a figure to itself.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student omits 270°, likely stopping at 180° and then jumping to 360° without checking the third multiple.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly includes 45°, perhaps halving the smallest angle without checking whether 45° actually produces coincidence.

inclusivity.support: Have the student physically rotate a cut-out windmill in 90° steps, pausing after each to check coincidence, and list each angle that works.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if a figure's smallest angle of symmetry is 90°, what is the order of its rotational symmetry, and how many times does it coincide with itself in one full turn?

exercise.description: Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point — sub-parts (a), (b), (c).

items.prompt: A 12-sector circle has alternate sectors coloured (sectors 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 are red; sectors 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 are white). How many angles of symmetry does this coloured figure have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — 6. The alternating pattern repeats every 2 sectors, so the smallest angle of symmetry is 360°/6 = 60°, giving 6 angles: 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The alternating two-sector pattern divides the circle into 6 identical units of 60° each; angles of symmetry are all multiples of 60° up to 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts the 12 sectors without recognising that the alternating colouring reduces the effective unit to every 2 sectors.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have divided 12 by 4 rather than correctly identifying the repeating unit as 2 sectors giving 6 repetitions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have confused 'angles of symmetry' with 'lines of symmetry' or only counted 180° and 360°.

inclusivity.support: Guide the student to draw the 12-sector circle, colour it as described, then rotate a tracing paper copy in steps to find coincidences.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: what colouring of the 12-sector circle gives exactly 4 angles of symmetry? Justify using the 360°/n reasoning.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: Colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has (i) 3 angles of symmetry, (ii) 4 angles of symmetry; (iii) determine all possible numbers of angles of symmetry obtainable by colouring sectors.

items.prompt: A figure has 60° as an angle of symmetry. It also has exactly two angles of symmetry that are smaller than 60°. What is the smallest angle of symmetry of this figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 20°. The smallest angle must be a factor of 60° and also a factor of 360°. If the smallest angle is s, then 60°/s = 3 (so there are exactly two angles smaller than 60°: s and 2s). Solving: s = 20°. Check: 20° is a factor of 360° (360/20 = 18). The angles smaller than 60° are 20° and 40°, giving exactly two.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest; if two multiples fall below 60°, then 60° = 3s, so s = 20°, verified as a factor of 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student set 60° = 2s (one angle below 60°) rather than three multiples (two below 60°), giving s = 30°.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student used 60° = 4s giving s = 15°, which would produce three angles below 60° (15°, 30°, 45°), not two.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student computed 360°/30 = 12° or used another unrelated divisor without checking the condition about two angles below 60°.

inclusivity.support: Write out the multiples of a trial value and count how many fall below 60° before settling on the answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Pose a variant: a figure has 72° as an angle of symmetry and exactly three angles smaller than 72°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

items.prompt: The outer boundary of a figure has 3 lines of reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry with smallest angle 120°. Which real-world structure does this description match, as discussed in the chapter?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The Parliament Building of India. Its circular outer boundary with three equally-spaced wings gives 3 lines of reflection symmetry and rotational angles of 120°, 240°, 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A figure with 3 equally-spaced features has smallest angle 360°/3 = 120° and 3 lines of symmetry; the Parliament Building matches this description as stated in the textbook.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates 4 blades with 4-fold symmetry (smallest angle 90°), not 3-fold; a correct instinct applied to the wrong example.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may know the Ashoka Chakra has many spokes (24) giving a much smaller angle of symmetry, not 120°.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows a regular hexagon has 6 lines and smallest angle 60°, so this correctly has 3-fold symmetry but refers to a geometric shape, not the real-world structure the question asks about.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to look at the Parliament Building image in the textbook and count the prominent wings of the circular building.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student how many angles of symmetry the Ashoka Chakra has, and what the smallest one is, based on its 24 spokes.

items.prompt: A student arranges 16 colour tiles in a 4 × 4 grid. The arrangement has exactly 2 lines of symmetry. Which pair of lines could these be?

options.label: A
options.text: The vertical centre line and the horizontal centre line

options.label: C
options.text: One diagonal and the vertical centre line

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — The vertical centre line and the horizontal centre line. These are the two axes of symmetry that can act independently in a rectangular grid without forcing the diagonals to also become lines of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a 4 × 4 grid, the vertical and horizontal centre lines can each be lines of symmetry without making the diagonals so, whereas if both diagonals are lines of symmetry the other axes are forced as well for a square arrangement.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may assume diagonal symmetry is easier to achieve, but in a square 4 × 4 grid, both diagonals being symmetry lines tends to force the axes as well, giving more than 2 lines.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student mixes one diagonal with one axis; this combination is geometrically possible in principle but in a square grid typically forces at least one more symmetry line.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student names only one line, which would give exactly 1 line of symmetry, not 2.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use square paper to colour a 4 × 4 grid and physically fold along each candidate line to check overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Challenge the student to colour a 4 × 4 grid so that it has exactly 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry, then justify why no second line exists.

items.section_title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry
items.prompt: Priya says, 'The diagonal of any rectangle is a line of symmetry because it passes through the centre and divides the rectangle into two equal triangles.' Is Priya correct? Explain your reasoning using the definition of a line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is not correct. A line of symmetry requires that when the figure is folded along that line, the two halves overlap exactly. When a non-square rectangle is folded along its diagonal, the two triangular halves do not coincide with the rectangular outline — the corners do not map onto each other correctly. Equal area and passing through the centre are not sufficient conditions; exact overlap on folding is the only criterion.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-overlap definition: label the corners of the rectangle, trace where each corner maps under the diagonal fold, and show that the mapped positions fall outside the rectangle's boundary.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to fold an actual rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal and observe whether the two parts coincide.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: for which rectangle (if any) does the diagonal become a line of symmetry, and why? Justify with a corner-mapping argument.

exercise.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'Any figure that has rotational symmetry must also have at least one line of reflection symmetry.' Using examples from the chapter, either prove this claim is true or give a counterexample that shows it is false. Explain your reasoning clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The claim is false. A counterexample is the paper windmill discussed in the chapter: it has rotational symmetry with angles of symmetry 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°, but it has no line of reflection symmetry — folding along any line does not produce exact overlap. This shows that rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry are independent properties; a figure can have one without the other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the windmill as having rotational symmetry (four angles) but no reflection symmetry (no fold produces exact overlap), disproving the claim by counterexample.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to first list the symmetry properties of the windmill (from the chapter) and then check whether any fold of the windmill produces exact overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct a second counterexample — a different figure with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry — and justify both properties.

items.prompt: A square sheet of paper is folded once along its vertical centre line. A single hole is then punched at a point that is 3 cm from the fold and 2 cm from the top edge. When the sheet is unfolded, how many holes appear, and where is each hole located? Describe the positions relative to the fold line and the top edge.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two holes appear. The original hole is 3 cm to the right of the fold line (or left, depending on which half was punched) and 2 cm from the top edge. Its reflection is the same distance on the other side of the fold line — 3 cm to the left (or right) — and also 2 cm from the top edge. The fold line (the vertical centre line) is the line of symmetry of the resulting two-hole pattern.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each point reflects across the fold line by reproducing the same perpendicular distance on the opposite side; the fold line is the line of symmetry of the unfolded pattern.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a square on squared paper, mark the fold line, plot the original hole, and count squares to find the mirror position.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the paper had been folded twice (vertical then horizontal) before punching one hole, how many holes would appear on unfolding, and describe all their positions.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: A square sheet of paper is folded in half (top half onto bottom half). A triangular cut is then made by cutting from the midpoint of the left edge to the midpoint of the bottom edge of the folded piece. When the paper is unfolded, what is the shape of the hole? How many lines of symmetry does the hole shape have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hole is a rhombus (a four-sided figure with all sides equal). The triangular cut on the folded piece produces a mirror-image triangle on the other half when unfolded, so the two triangles together form a rhombus. The rhombus has 2 lines of symmetry: one along the horizontal fold line and one vertical line through its two pointed vertices.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The fold reflects the triangular cut to the other half; the unfolded hole is the union of the triangle and its mirror image — a rhombus with 2 lines of symmetry.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to make the actual cut on paper and observe the shape directly, then identify the fold line as one line of symmetry.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the same paper had been folded twice (in half horizontally then in half vertically) and the same triangular cut made, what shape would the hole be and how many lines of symmetry would it have?

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: Describe the sequence of folds and the single straight cut needed to produce a square hole whose sides are aligned with the sides of the original sheet. How is your folding sequence different from the one that produces a square hole rotated 45° (diamond orientation)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: For an aligned-square hole: fold the paper along both the vertical and horizontal centre lines (two folds), then make a single straight cut parallel to a side of the folded piece — this cut, when unfolded, produces a square hole with sides parallel to the sheet's sides. For the diamond-orientation (45°-rotated) square hole: fold along both diagonals instead, then make a single straight cut; unfolding produces a square hole rotated 45° relative to the sheet. The key difference is that aligned folds (axis-parallel) produce axis-aligned holes, while diagonal folds produce diagonally-oriented holes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The orientation of the hole mirrors the orientation of the fold axes; axis-parallel folds give an aligned hole, diagonal folds give a rotated (diamond) hole.

inclusivity.support: Guide the student to first make the aligned-square hole by folding and cutting, open it, observe the result, then try the diagonal fold version.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: could a single fold (not two) produce a square hole? If yes, describe the fold and cut; if no, explain why two folds are needed.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: An arrangement of identical rhombus tiles on a grid is described as follows: three rhombuses are placed so that they share a common vertex at the centre, each rotated 120° from the next. How many lines of symmetry does the resulting figure have? State each line's orientation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The figure has 3 lines of symmetry. Each line of symmetry passes through the shared central vertex and through the midpoint of the opposite side of one rhombus (or equivalently, bisects the angle between two adjacent rhombuses). The three lines are equally spaced at 120° to each other — they are oriented at 60°, 180°, and 300° from a horizontal reference (or equivalently at 0°, 120°, 240° depending on the starting orientation of the rhombuses).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A figure with 3 identical units arranged at 120° intervals has 3-fold symmetry: 3 lines of reflection, each passing through the centre and bisecting one unit, equally spaced at 120°.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to trace the three-rhombus figure and physically fold along each candidate line to check whether it produces overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: does this three-rhombus figure also have rotational symmetry? If so, state the angles of symmetry and connect them to the number of units using the 360°/n formula.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: On squared paper, a partial figure is given: it consists of an L-shaped set of 5 squares. The figure has a vertical line of symmetry and also a horizontal line of symmetry. How many additional squares must be added to complete the figure, and on which sides of the L-shape must they be placed?
items.visual_stimulus: number_line: Original L (5 sq) | + vertical mirror | + horizontal mirror | = Complete figure

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The L-shape has 5 squares on one side of both lines of symmetry. Reflecting horizontally adds 5 squares to make the L symmetric about the vertical axis; that reflected shape is then reflected about the horizontal axis, adding another 10 squares. The complete figure therefore requires 15 additional squares (total figure: 20 squares). The additional squares are placed: 5 on the right of the original L (vertical mirror), 5 below the original L (horizontal mirror), and 5 in the diagonally opposite corner (both mirrors). Exact placement depends on the specific L-shape described, but the principle is that each quadrant must be a mirror of the others.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply each line of symmetry in turn: reflect the original across the vertical axis, then reflect the combined figure across the horizontal axis, ensuring all four quadrants are mirror images.

inclusivity.support: Provide squared paper and ask the student to first draw the vertical mirror image of the L, then apply the horizontal mirror to the combined shape.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the completed figure (with both lines of symmetry) also happens to have rotational symmetry, what is the smallest angle of rotational symmetry? Justify using the chapter's method.
